title: Connect Hub to your identity provider
description: Understand domain-based OIDC sign-in, matching Hub accounts and the additional boundary of SSO chaining.

chapters.title: Sign-in and Hub access remain distinct

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Imagine a fictional company that already manages staff sign-in through an identity provider. Can Hub use that instead of asking everyone to maintain another password?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Yes. Hub can use OpenID Connect, usually shortened to OIDC. A configured domain directs sign-in to the relevant provider. After authentication and verification, Hub locates the matching local user account.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Does a successful provider login automatically create the right camera access?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: No. The guide requires a matching Hub user. Authentication establishes identity; Hub still needs its own account, role and resource configuration. Don't confuse an identity provider accepting someone with that person being entitled to every recording.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Our administrator chooses Microsoft Entra. Is the setup only a Hub-side switch?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: No. Register the application with the provider and configure the corresponding issuer, client settings, identity claim and callback information in Hub. The callback must match the intended deployment. Keep client secrets in the appropriate protected configuration.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Could the same basic idea work with another OIDC provider?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Yes. The provider's interface differs, but the agreement about the application and redirect destination still matters. Test a known matching user through the actual public sign-in route rather than only checking that a client identifier exists.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Suppose the company embeds Hub inside another application that's already signed in. Is that just the same flow again?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The guide calls this SSO chaining. The surrounding application performs authentication and passes the relevant token to Hub's verification flow. Hub needs the correct provider definition and verification client configuration for that application.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: So being inside an iframe doesn't itself make the browser session trusted?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Exactly. Treat chaining as a separate integration with explicit validation. Use the linked guide for the exact contract, protect tokens from exposure, and don't substitute an unverified identity just to make an embedded login feel seamless.

chapters.title: Test before enforcing the sign-in choice

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Can the administrator make the provider the default experience for a domain?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The documented Force SSO setting shows the provider redirection and hides the ordinary username and password fields on that domain page. Verify the complete sign-in route before changing what users see.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Match the provider application and callback, confirm the Hub account, test the user's actual resource access, and test chaining independently if you use it. Central sign-in is useful, but it doesn't replace careful authorization inside Hub.

editorialStyle.tone: A short, high-level introduction for a first-time listener. Explain why the topic matters, build one mental model, and suggest one next action. Sound like two colleagues, not a narrated manual.
editorialStyle.scope: Aim for four to five minutes and roughly 500-550 spoken words. Use one fictional example and four short chapters. Leave identifiers, form limits, configuration, migration mechanics, and troubleshooting checklists in the linked guide. Keep essential caveats as practical consequences.
editorialStyle.humour: Optional: one or two brief, relevant light moments are enough. Prefer a relatable analogy over a separate joke. Never pad the overview with banter.
editorialStyle.reactions: Use occasional short, natural responses such as 'Oh, that makes sense' or 'Wait, so...' followed by a real question. Avoid repetitive praise, canned agreement, and filler.
editorialStyle.laughter: Optional: at most one or two light reactions such as 'Ha, fair point.' Never insert [laughs], SSML, or repeated ha-ha strings. These are spoken reactions, not a guarantee of genuine laughter from the current speech engine.
editorialStyle.intonation: Write real questions with question marks, use contractions, alternate short and longer sentences, and make contrasts explicit. Let punctuation and sentence rhythm suggest curiosity, surprise, and emphasis. Avoid all-caps shouting, excessive exclamation marks, and artificial pause tags.
editorialStyle.guardrails: Keep technical claims source-backed. Never mock the listener, joke about real victims, minimize security or data-loss risks, or let humour replace an explanation. Personality is optional; accuracy and clarity are not.
